answer.label: Not Helena Blavatsky — a Quote Investigator headline
answer.sourceLine: This phrase is not a quotation at all. It is the title Quote Investigator gave its 20 April 2015 investigation ↗ into a whole family of sayings about chance, coincidence and God — a list of the article’s themes, not words anyone spoke. Blavatsky’s real link to the subject is a single sentence in The Secret Doctrine (1888), where she quotes “Chance is but the pseudonym of God (or Nature)…” and credits Coleridge; the saying is in fact Théophile Gautier’s, written in 1845.

source.heading: What the words actually are

docMeta.dd: Quote Origin: Chance, Coincidence, Miracles, Pseudonyms, and God
Quote Investigator, 20 April 2015 — an article headline, not a quotation
La Croix de Berny: Roman Steeple-Chase, Letter 3 (1845)
The Secret Doctrine, vol. 1, p. 653 (London, 1888) — quoted there, credited to Coleridge

source.excerpt: Most certainly chance is “impossible.” There is no “chance” in Nature, wherein everything is mathematically co-ordinate and mutually related in its units. “Chance,” says Coleridge, “is but the pseudonym of God (or Nature), for those particular cases which He does not choose to subscribe openly with His sign manual.” Replace the word “God” by that of Karma and it will become an Eastern axiom.
trail: 1845 — Théophile Gautier writes the sentence in Letter 3 of La Croix de Berny, signed with the fictional name Edgard de Meilhan: “Le hasard, c’est peut-être le pseudonyme de Dieu, quand il ne veut pas signer.” ↗

1847 — Thomas De Quincey carries it into English, crediting only an unnamed Frenchman: “Chance is but the pseudonym of God for those particular cases which he does not choose to subscribe openly with his own sign manual.” ↗

1888 — Helena Blavatsky quotes that English sentence in The Secret Doctrine, vol. 1, p. 653 ↗, attributing it to Coleridge and adding: “Replace the word ‘God’ by that of Karma and it will become an Eastern axiom.”

2015 — Quote Investigator maps the whole chain — Walpole, Chamfort, Gautier, De Quincey, Coleridge, Blavatsky, Anatole France, Doris Lessing, Einstein — under the headline “Chance, Coincidence, Miracles, Pseudonyms, and God” ↗. That headline is what later got circulated as a quotation.
source.excerptNote: This is the passage Blavatsky actually wrote — the only place in her work where the words of the headline overlap with hers. The string “Chance, Coincidence, Miracles, Pseudonyms, and God” appears nowhere in her writing; it is Quote Investigator’s own summary title for the tangle of sayings this sentence belongs to.

author.name: Théophile Gautier
author.heading: Who Théophile Gautier was
author.bio: Théophile Gautier was a French poet, dramatist, novelist, journalist and art critic, born at Tarbes in 1811 and died at Neuilly-sur-Seine in 1872. He was a central figure of French Romanticism and later a standard-bearer for l’art pour l’art, admired by Baudelaire and Flaubert. The line about chance comes from a piece of literary play: La Croix de Berny was a novel written in letters by four authors in rotation, and Gautier wrote the letters signed “Edgard de Meilhan” — which is part of why the sentence spent decades circulating with no name attached to it at all.

misattribution.heading: Four wrong names, and one line that is real
misattribution.intro: This one is unusual. The string being passed around is not a misquotation of Blavatsky — it is not a quotation at all. Underneath it sits a genuine sentence, and that sentence has collected a remarkable run of wrong names.

items.why: “Chance, Coincidence, Miracles, Pseudonyms, and God” is the title Quote Investigator ↗ put on its 2015 article — a list of the themes it examines. Blavatsky is one of a dozen names weighed inside it, alongside Walpole, Chamfort, Gautier, De Quincey, Coleridge, Anatole France, Doris Lessing and Einstein.

Blavatsky credited Coleridge in The Secret Doctrine (1888). Quote Investigator ↗ reports that the Coleridge ascription first appears in Henry Southgate’s 1862 compilation Many Thoughts of Many Minds, p. 81, and that it has located no substantive support for it; Coleridge had died in 1834. English readers had already met the sentence in 1847 credited to nobody in particular.

From Hoyt’s New Cyclopedia of Practical Quotations (1923) onward — through Evan Esar’s dictionary (1949), F. P. Adams (1952) and the 1968 Bartlett’s — Gautier’s sentence was printed under Anatole France’s name, per Quote Investigator ↗. France did write a related but different line in Le Jardin d’Épicure: “Chance, in the last resort, is God.”

“Coincidence is God’s way of remaining anonymous” was spoken by Charlotte Clemensen Taylor in a 1986 Associated Press story, credited to Doris Lessing in 1997, and only attached to Einstein in a book published in 2000. Quote Investigator ↗ notes it is absent from The Ultimate Quotable Einstein.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence at the bottom of all of it belongs to Théophile Gautier, written in 1845 for Letter 3 of La Croix de Berny: “Le hasard, c’est peut-être le pseudonyme de Dieu, quand il ne veut pas signer.” ↗

context.heading: How a headline becomes a quotation
lead: Quote sites scrape. When a researcher writes an article called “Chance, Coincidence, Miracles, Pseudonyms, and God” and fills it with famous names, a scraper that cannot tell a heading from a sentence will lift the heading and pin it to whichever name sits nearest. Blavatsky is a natural landing spot: she is a magnet for unsourced spiritual-sounding lines, and she really does appear in that article.

What she appears there for is worth knowing on its own. In The Secret Doctrine she uses the saying to argue something close to the opposite of what it sounds like — not that God hides behind coincidence, but that nothing is coincidental. “There is no ‘chance’ in Nature,” she writes, and then swaps the word: replace God with Karma, she says, and it becomes an Eastern axiom. She was borrowing a French epigram to make a point about universal law — and she got the borrowing wrong, crediting Coleridge for a line no one has shown Coleridge wrote.
detailsBody: 1777 Horace Walpole: “What is called chance is the instrument of Providence.” 1795 Chamfort plays with Providence as chance’s baptismal name. 1845 Gautier writes the pseudonym line. 1847 Alexis de Valon reprints it as the words of “someone”; De Quincey renders it in English as the words of “a Frenchman.”

1855–1856 It circulates anonymously in a footnote to Bacon’s Novum Organum and in an anthology of spare-moment reading. 1862 Southgate attaches Coleridge’s name. 1886–1888 The Coleridge credit spreads, and Blavatsky repeats it.

1923–1968 Reference works swap in Anatole France. 1976–1986 A separate American strand adds “miracle” and “anonymous,” ending in Charlotte Clemensen Taylor’s 1986 phrasing. 1997 Doris Lessing gets the credit. 2000 Einstein does. All of it is documented, with citations, at Quote Investigator ↗.

sourcesVerified.claim: "Chance, Coincidence, Miracles, Pseudonyms, and God" is the title of a Quote Investigator article (full title: "Quote Origin: Chance, Coincidence, Miracles, Pseudonyms, and God"), dated 20 April 2015 in its URL. It documents the chain: Walpole 1777, Chamfort 1795, Gautier 1845 (La Croix de Berny, 1855 printing, quote p. 28), de Valon 1847, De Quincey May 1847 in Tait's Edinburgh Magazine vol. 14 pp. 328-29, an anonymous 1855 Novum Organum footnote, an 1856 anthology, Southgate 1862 attaching Coleridge (Many Thoughts of Many Minds, p. 81), Ballou 1886, Blavatsky 1888 (The Secret Doctrine vol. 1, p. 653, Theosophical Publishing Company, London), Anatole France 1895/1922, Hoyt's 1923, Esar 1949, F. P. Adams 1952, Bartlett's 1968, Paul F. 1976, Shop with Sue 1979, Heidi Quade 1984, Bonnie Farmer 1985, Charlotte Clemensen Taylor 1986 (AP), Doris Lessing 1997, Einstein 2000. QI states it has located no substantive support for the Coleridge ascription (Coleridge died in 1834) and no substantive evidence Einstein used the saying, noting it is absent from The Ultimate Quotable Einstein.

French Wikisource's text of La Croix de Berny, Letter 3 (Librairie nouvelle, 1855, pp. 26-38; work dated 1845), signed by the character Edgard de Meilhan, contains verbatim: "Vous auriez tort de vouloir forcer la main au hasard ; laissez-le agir, il sait bien mieux que vous ce qu'il vous faut. — Le hasard, c'est peut-être le pseudonyme de Dieu, quand il ne veut pas signer." The work is credited to Delphine de Girardin, Théophile Gautier, Jules Sandeau and Joseph Méry.

The Theosophical University Press online edition of The Secret Doctrine contains, immediately after the page marker "Vol. 1, Page 653": "Most certainly chance is 'impossible.' There is no 'chance' in Nature, wherein everything is mathematically co-ordinate and mutually related in its units. 'Chance,' says Coleridge, 'is but the pseudonym of God (or Nature), for those particular cases which He does not choose to subscribe openly with His sign manual.' Replace the word 'God' by that of Karma and it will become an Eastern axiom."

The Internet Archive full text of De Quincey's "The Spanish Military Nun" contains: "Or, as a Frenchman says, with eloquent ingenuity, in connexion with this very story, 'Chance is but the pseudonym of God for those particular cases which he does not choose to subscribe openly with his own sign manual.'" — De Quincey credits an unnamed Frenchman, not Coleridge.

Théophile Gautier was born 30 August 1811 in Tarbes and died 23 October 1872 at Neuilly-sur-Seine; the opening sentence describes him as "a French poet, dramatist, novelist, journalist, and art and literary critic."

Helena Blavatsky was born 12 August 1831 and died 8 May 1891; she is described as a Russian and American mystic and writer who co-founded the Theosophical Society in 1875, and The Secret Doctrine was published in 1888.

CONTROL CHECK (deliberately negative): the English Wikiquote page for Samuel Taylor Coleridge does NOT contain the saying "Chance is but the pseudonym of God" in any section, so this dossier makes no Wikiquote section-label claim (Misattributed/Disputed) about it.
